Euler Nagel In Quad

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four special dots from a four-sided shape always sit on one straight line.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show more centre lines, and press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

A triangle has four famous centre points that always share a line. Give a quadrilateral four corners and it makes four triangles — and four copies of each centre. Join the copies made by opposite corners and something surprising stays true, however you drag the shape.

The line inside one triangle

In any triangle the orthocenter H, the nine-point center N, the centroid G and the circumcenter O lie on Euler's line, in that order. N is the midpoint of HO, so HN : NO = 1 : 1; G is two thirds of the way from H to O, so HG : GO = 2 : 1. The logic test confirms this in each of the four triangles for every shape it tries.

Four copies of each centre

Write HA for the orthocenter of the triangle BCD that leaves out A, and do the same for N, G and O. The page defines H' = HAHC ∩ HBHD, and likewise N', G' and O'. Its main claim (1') is that in any quadrilateral these four new points are collinear, with H'N' : N'O' = 1 : 1 and H'G' : G'O' = 2 : 1. O' is simply where the diagonals AC and BD cross. The test checks this independently with ordinary line algebra on thousands of random shapes, including crossed and non-convex ones; the ratios hold to within rounding error.

When the corners lie on a circle

For a cyclic quadrilateral the four circumcentres coincide at the circle's centre, and the four centre quadrilaterals are homothetic with ABCD. The page's claim (2) is that their three homothety centres H, N, G and the common O lie in that order with HN : NO = 1 : 2 and HG : GO = 1 : 1 — different from both (1) and (1'). The test confirms these exact thirds and halves on two thousand random cyclic quadrilaterals.

Why the ratios travel

Write D as D = xA + yB + zC with x + y + z = 1. The map that sends ABC to its three centre points is an affine map, so it sends D to the centre of the triangle that omits D. It therefore keeps every division ratio: since each triangle has HG : GO = 2 : 1, the same ratio holds between the matching copies, and the intersection of the diagonals maps to the intersection of the copy lines. That is why dragging one corner never changes the proportions. The port copies the applet's drawing quirk too: it snaps two centres less than one unit apart to their midpoint, so a nearly flat shape may show a slightly shifted dot even though the theorem is exact.

Tick all six boxes, then drag the corners until all four sit on one circle: watch the line change from the 1:1 and 2:1 pattern to the 1:2 and 1:1 pattern.
